section.title: Revive Us Again
section.sectionRationale: A communal prayer of the sons of Korah near the close of Book III, this psalm looks back to a past forgiveness and restoration, then pleads for a fresh revival, and closes with a vision of steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace meeting together in the land, a hope that anticipates the mercy and justice that meet fully at the cross.
section.thesis: Israel calls on the God who once forgave and restored her to revive her again, trusting that His steadfast love and faithfulness, His righteousness and peace, will meet and kiss, a hope fulfilled when Christ, in whom mercy and truth embrace, goes before His people to prepare the way.
section.frameNote: Four movements: remembering God's past forgiveness and restraint of wrath, verses 1-3; pleading for renewed favor and revival, verses 4-7; listening for the LORD's word of peace, verses 8-9; and a vision of loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace meeting to bless the land, verses 10-13.

verses.text: You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity.
You forgave the iniquity of Your people; You covered all their sin. Selah
You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger.
Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us.
Will You be angry with us forever? Will You draw out Your anger to all generations?
Will You not {{chayah|revive}} us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?
Show us Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}, O LORD, and grant us Your salvation.
I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints; He will not let them return to folly.
Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him, that His glory may dwell in our land.
Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and {{shalom|peace}} have kissed.
Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.
The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase.
{{tsedeq|Righteousness}} will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps.

chayah.gloss: To live, to be revived, to be brought back to life. The psalmist asks God to breathe fresh life into a people who once knew forgiveness but now need renewal again.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant love and loyal devotion. The psalmist appeals to this quality of God as the ground for hoping in a fresh act of salvation.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, completeness. Here peace is personified as meeting and embracing righteousness, picturing the full reconciliation God's salvation brings.

tsedeq.gloss: Righteousness, rightness. Righteousness is pictured as a herald walking ahead of the LORD, preparing the way for His coming, language later applied to the forerunner of the Messiah.

basic.context: Sung by the sons of Korah, this psalm remembers a time when God forgave His people's sin and restored them, then turns to plead for that same mercy again. It closes with a beautiful picture of God's love, truth, righteousness, and peace all meeting together to bless the land.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes a specific season of national sin, judgment, and partial restoration, and it prescribes an abiding pattern: remember God's past grace, confess present need honestly, and wait for His word of peace rather than manufacturing your own relief.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist asks God to chayah, revive or bring back to life, His discouraged people, verse 6. He appeals to chesed, God's steadfast covenant love, verse 7. And in the psalm's climax, shalom, peace, meets tsedeq, righteousness, in a kiss, verse 10, while righteousness itself goes before the LORD to prepare His way, verse 13.
basic.typology: The meeting of loving devotion and faithfulness, righteousness and peace, in verse 10 pictures what happens fully at the cross, where God's justice and mercy embrace. And righteousness going before the LORD to prepare His way, verse 13, anticipates the forerunner who prepares the way of the Lord before Christ's coming.
basic.christ: At the cross, God's righteousness and peace truly kiss: His justice against sin and His mercy toward sinners meet in the death and resurrection of Jesus, so that He is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith, Romans 3:25-26. Christ Himself is our peace, Ephesians 2:14, the answer to this psalm's longing for revival and reconciliation.
basic.god: God is shown as one who has forgiven and restrained His wrath before, and who can be trusted to do so again. He does not hold His anger forever; He listens, speaks peace, and provides what is good, while never asking His people to abandon righteousness to receive it.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:25-26 shows God's righteousness and mercy meeting in Christ's atoning death. Isaiah 40:3 and Matthew 3:3 show righteousness, in the person of a forerunner, preparing the way of the Lord. Ephesians 2:14 names Christ Himself as our peace.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's plea for revival and its vision of love, truth, righteousness, and peace meeting together find their answer in Christ, in whom God's justice and mercy kiss at the cross, and who goes before His people to prepare the way into God's presence.

context.literary:
Psalm 85 is built in three panels, and each panel has its own tense. Verses 1 to 3 are in the perfect, a string of past acts: You showed favour, You restored, You forgave, You covered, You withheld, You turned. Verses 4 to 7 change to imperatives and questions: Restore us, put away, will You be angry, will You not revive. Verses 8 to 13 move into the future and into a different voice, first the singer who resolves to listen, then the oracle he hears or expects, and then a vision in which nothing is asked because everything is promised. The psalm therefore moves in time from what God has done, to what the people need now, to what God will surely do.

A single Hebrew verb, shuv, to turn or return, holds the poem together. It is the root behind God's restoring in verse 1, His turning from anger in verse 3, the plea "Restore us" in verse 4, the question "Will You not revive us again" in verse 6, where the sense is "turn and revive," and the warning that His people must not "return to folly" in verse 8. Five times the same movement of turning appears in five different verses, sometimes as God's act and sometimes as the people's need. The psalm asks a question about who turns first, and the answer offered is that God's turning makes ours possible.

The centre of the poem is the group of verses 10 to 13, which is arranged as a set of pairs. Verse 10 pairs love with faithfulness and righteousness with peace. Verse 11 pairs earth with heaven, as faithfulness sprouts upward and righteousness looks downward. Verse 12 pairs the LORD's giving with the land's yielding. Verse 13 ends with righteousness going ahead and a path opening behind it. The lines form a frame of meeting, then exchange, then harvest, then walking. The verbs of movement are chosen carefully. The first verb of verse 10 is the ordinary Hebrew word for meeting someone on a road, and that suggests the virtues have set out from opposite directions and arrived at the same place.
context.historical:
The psalm looks back on a restoration and forward to a fuller one, and the most natural home for that combination is the years after the exile. When Cyrus of Persia issued his proclamation in the first year of his reign, those who belonged to God's people were told to go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD, Ezra 1:1-3. The first return brought a real turning: Jeremiah had spoken of a day when God would restore the fortunes of Jacob's tents, Jeremiah 30:18, and now it had happened. Yet the small community that came back found that restoration was not the same as flourishing.

The prophets of those years describe the disappointment. Haggai says the people had planted much but harvested little, that they earned wages to put into a bag pierced through, and that the heavens had withheld their dew and the earth its crops, Haggai 1:6 and 1:10-11. When the foundation of the second temple was laid, many shouted for joy while the older ones, who had seen the first house, wept, and the sound of joy and weeping could not be told apart, Ezra 3:10-13. Nehemiah's prayer describes a generation that was back in the land yet still in distress, slaves in the land God had given, with its harvest going to foreign kings, Nehemiah 9:36-37. A worshipper in that situation could sing verses 1 to 3 with gratitude and verses 4 to 7 with ache.

The prayer for the land to yield its increase, verse 12, also draws on the covenant blessings. The law promised that if Israel kept faith, God would give rain in its season and the land would yield its produce, Leviticus 26:3-4 and Deuteronomy 11:13-15, and the prophets after the exile promised the same, Zechariah 8:12. The psalm is thus not a general reflection on forgiveness but a very particular prayer for a real community: forgive, and then let the fields answer. Some readers connect the psalm with an earlier crisis instead, and the debate below sets out the options.
context.canonical:
Psalm 85 sits among the psalms of communal lament and restoration. Its refrain-like plea, "Restore us," has close relatives in Psalm 80:3 and 80:19, where the prayer is repeated with growing intensity: "Restore us, O LORD God of Hosts; cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved." Psalm 60:1 opens with a similar cry. Psalm 126:1-6 provides the mirror image: "When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers," followed by a prayer to restore them further, like streams in the Negev. The pattern of thanking God for a past turning and asking for a further one is a standard shape in Israel's worship.

Verses 2 and 3 draw on the words God used to describe Himself at Sinai. Exodus 34:6-7 proclaims a God abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Moses appealed to the same words in Numbers 14:18-19 when he begged pardon for a rebellious people. Psalm 85:2 speaks of God lifting away iniquity and covering sin, the same pair as in Psalm 32:1, and Psalm 103:8-12 unfolds the same character. The two words that appear together in verse 10, loving devotion and faithfulness, are the very pair in the Sinai formula, so that verse 10 is not a fresh idea but a return to the heart of Israel's creed.

The promise of verse 11, faithfulness sprouting from earth and righteousness looking down from heaven, echoes Isaiah 45:8, where the skies pour down righteousness and the earth opens so that salvation may sprout. Hosea 2:21-22 pictures heaven and earth answering one another, and Isaiah 32:15-17 says that the work of righteousness will be peace. In the New Testament, John says that the Word became flesh and was full of grace and truth, John 1:14, and that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1:17. The words are those of verse 10 in another language. Paul's account of how God stays righteous while justifying sinners, Romans 3:21-26, and his statement that we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, Romans 5:1, read like a long commentary on the same verse.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Korahite author, speaking for a people who have already been forgiven once and yet are again in trouble, wanted the community to learn a way of praying when God's favour seems half given. The lesson has three steps. First, remember: the psalm begins by recounting what God has done, not what the people feel. Second, ask boldly: the questions "Will You be angry with us forever?" show that the faithful are permitted to press God with His own character. Third, wait for an answer rather than inventing one: the singer says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say."

The author also meant the people to hear a warning inside the promise. God will speak peace to His people, but He will not let them return to folly, verse 8. Restoration without repentance would be an empty thing, and the promise is for those who fear Him, verse 9. The closing vision then answers what all the earlier verses wanted: a land where God's character is not only heard about but seen at home. The author intends the reader to finish the psalm not with the last request but with a picture, so that hope has a shape and can be held.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one community's history and its prayer. The forgiveness of verses 2 and 3 and the harvest of verse 12 are things God did or would do for Israel in that land; they are not a promise that every believing nation will have good crops. To read verse 12 as a guarantee of material prosperity for anyone who prays this psalm would go beyond the text, which places the harvest after forgiveness and inside the covenant with Israel. The prophets themselves show that the fields did not always answer, as Haggai 1:6 makes plain.

The psalm prescribes a way of praying and a set of priorities. Begin with what God has done, name what still needs mending, listen for His word, and expect that mercy and truth, righteousness and peace belong together and will not be pulled apart. The warning of verse 8, that God's people must not return to folly, is a direct instruction for anyone who has received mercy. Paul asks the same question in a New Testament key: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? Romans 6:1. The psalm's own answer is that peace is given to those who fear the LORD and turn from folly, not to those who use forgiveness as licence.

debates.question: What situation lies behind the restoration described in verses 1 to 3?

views.label: The return from Babylonian exile under Cyrus
views.case: Verse 1 can be translated 'restored the fortunes of Jacob,' as the BSB footnote notes, and Jeremiah 30:18 uses similar words of the return from exile. The tension between a past restoration and a present plea for revival fits the early years of the return, when the harvests were poor, Haggai 1:6, and the temple looked like nothing next to the old one, Haggai 2:3.

views.label: An earlier deliverance from judgment, such as relief after a national disaster
views.case: The language of forgiveness and of turning from burning anger could describe any occasion when God relented, and nothing in the psalm names Babylon. Psalms 60 and 80 also plead for restoration after military disaster, with no mention of exile.

views.label: A prophetic perfect: the past tenses describe what the psalmist is certain God will do
views.case: Hebrew poets sometimes use the perfect tense for events they treat as so sure that they can speak of them as done. On this reading verses 1 to 3 are confidence spoken in advance, and verses 4 to 7 the prayer that grows out of that confidence. The difficulty is that verse 4 asks for restoration as if it had not yet come, so this view has to hold that the psalm mixes moods deliberately.

debates.bearing: Each view leaves the psalm's use unchanged. God's past mercy is the ground of present prayer, and present distress does not cancel past grace. The post-exilic reading gives the most coherent picture, but a reader who prefers another setting will still find that the psalm teaches the same pattern of remember, ask and listen.

debates.question: What does it mean that love and faithfulness 'met' and righteousness and peace 'kissed' in verse 10?

views.label: Four attributes of God at work together in the restored land
views.case: In the Sinai formula, loving devotion and faithfulness belong to God, Exodus 34:6, and Psalm 89:14 says they go before Him. Verse 10 then says that these qualities, along with righteousness and peace, are not rivals but partners, and the coming restoration will display all four together in the life of the nation.

views.label: A meeting of God's side and the people's side
views.case: Verse 11 speaks of faithfulness springing up from the earth and righteousness looking down from heaven. Some read the four virtues as split between heaven and earth, with God's love and righteousness coming down, and the people's faithfulness and peace rising up, so that restoration is a meeting between them.

views.label: A picture of justice and mercy reconciled, fulfilled at the cross
views.case: Christian readers since the early centuries have heard in verse 10 the gospel's answer to how God can be both just and merciful. Romans 3:25-26 speaks of God demonstrating His righteousness so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus. On this reading the psalm's picture is fulfilled, not simply illustrated, in the atonement.

debates.bearing: The first reading is closest to the psalm's own setting, and the third is the New Testament's development of it. The three do not compete so much as widen. Whatever the first hearers understood, they saw that mercy and truth are allies, and the church sees the ground of that alliance in the cross.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb that runs through the psalm is shuv, to turn or return, and the phrase in verse 1 that the BSB renders "restored Jacob from captivity" is literally shavta shevut Ya'akov, "You turned the turning of Jacob," which the BSB footnote gives as "restored the fortunes of Jacob." The noun shevut appears in a family of phrases about God reversing a people's condition, as in Jeremiah 30:18 and Psalm 126:1. Whether it means captivity or fortunes, it says that God has moved the community from a bad state to a good one. The same verb returns in verse 3, "You turned from Your burning anger," where God is the one who turns back from wrath; in verse 4, "Restore us," where the people ask Him to turn them; in verse 6, "Will You not revive us again," which begins with the verb "turn"; and in verse 8, where the faithful must not "return to folly." One root, many hands.

Verse 2 sets two verbs of forgiveness side by side. The first, nasa, means to lift or carry, and the picture is of God picking up the weight of iniquity and carrying it away. The second, kasah, means to cover. The pair also appears in Psalm 32:1, where the blessed man is one whose transgression is lifted away and whose sin is covered. The noun avon, iniquity, is the twisted or crooked thing, and chattat, sin, is the missing of the mark. Together with verse 3's "withheld all Your fury," using a verb of gathering in, asaph, the psalm shows God drawing back His anger as one draws in a hand.

In verse 5 the questions "forever" and "to all generations" use the words olam and dor vador, the largest time words in the language. The lament asks whether the anger is a permanent setting. Verse 7 then presents the answer the psalm seeks: "Show us Your loving devotion," where the verb is a causative of "to see." The people want to see chesed. The word "salvation" that follows, yesha, is from the root of Joshua's name, Yeshua, and carries the sense of a spacious deliverance.

In verse 8 the singer says, "I will listen," and then describes the message: God "will speak peace" to His people and to "His saints," chasidim, those who are the objects and practitioners of chesed. It is a word of belonging. The last clause, "He will not let them return to folly," uses kislah, a word for foolishness or misplaced confidence, and warns against the very turning the psalm has just celebrated in God. Verse 9 says that His glory "may dwell" in the land, using shakan, the verb that gives the Hebrew nouns mishkan, tabernacle, and, in later Jewish usage, shekinah. The glory that left the temple in Ezekiel's vision is being asked to settle again.

The great verse is verse 10. The BSB has "have joined together," but the Hebrew verb is nifgashu, from pagash, to meet or encounter, the word used for meeting a person on the road. Righteousness and peace "kissed," nashaqu, which is the verb of greeting and affection between family. In this verse both verbs are perfect, expressed as accomplished facts. The four words that meet are chesed, steadfast covenant love, emet, faithfulness or truth, tsedeq, righteousness, and shalom, wholeness or peace. The first pair is the pair from the Sinai formula, and the second pair is the pair of justice and well-being. John's Greek for grace and truth, charis and aletheia, the phrase in John 1:14 and 1:17, is widely heard as an echo of chesed and emet.

Verse 11 has faithfulness "sprouts" from the earth, from the verb tsamach, the ordinary verb for plants growing, while righteousness "looks down" from heaven, nishqaph, a verb of bending to look through a window or lattice. Verse 12 says the land will give its "increase," yevul, the produce of the fields. Verse 13 ends with tsedeq going before Him and setting itself "on the way of His steps," in the Hebrew, a phrase that is hard, since the verb "set" has no explicit object. Most translators supply "to prepare the way," which is the reading the BSB takes. Another way is to read it as righteousness making a path for His footsteps to follow, so that righteousness becomes the road on which God walks toward His people.

In the Septuagint, the noun for peace is eirene and for righteousness dikaiosyne, and Paul's letters, which use both, sit close to this psalm's vocabulary.

typology.type: The restoration remembered and hoped for, verses 1 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The people's past turning of fortunes, and their plea for another, take a definite shape in the pattern of exile and return. Jeremiah's promise that God would restore the fortunes of Jacob's tents, Jeremiah 30:18, was only partly seen in the first return, as Haggai and Ezra show. The New Testament claims that the deeper restoration has come in Christ, through whom we receive adoption as sons, Galatians 4:4-5, and the Spirit who makes alive, Titus 3:4-7. The escalation is from a return to a land to a return to God. The type is incomplete because the church still prays for revival, and Revelation 21:3 promises that the final restoration is yet to be revealed.

Israel's forgiveness in the psalm rests on God's own character and not on a reason the psalm supplies. The New Testament says how the lifting was done. God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice, so that He could pass over sins and still be righteous, Romans 3:25-26. Where the psalm speaks of covering, Paul says there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1, and that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The type falls short because the Old Testament covering was granted while the price was still unpaid.

typology.type: Loving devotion and faithfulness meeting, righteousness and peace kissing, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: This is the most striking correspondence in the psalm. Grace and truth, John 1:14 and 1:17, arrive together in the person of Jesus, and Paul speaks of peace made through the blood of the cross, Colossians 1:19-20, and says that Christ Himself is our peace, Ephesians 2:14. At the cross the demands of righteousness and the mercy of love are not traded off against each other; both are satisfied in one act. The psalm gives a picture, and the New Testament shows the mechanism. The picture is not exhausted by the cross, however, since it also looks toward a land where these virtues are plain in every relationship.

typology.type: Righteousness going before Him to prepare the way, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The psalm ends with righteousness as the herald of the LORD's coming. Isaiah 40:3-5 has a voice crying to prepare the way of the LORD, and the Gospels apply it to John the Baptist, Matthew 3:3, who was to go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him, Luke 1:76. Malachi 3:1 promises a messenger who will prepare the way. Christ then comes as the one whose coming brings peace to those far and near, Isaiah 57:19 and Ephesians 2:17. The type is not a perfect match: in the psalm righteousness is the forerunner, while in the Gospels a person is, and the righteousness the forerunner announces is found in the Lord who follows.

study.christ:
The psalm points to Christ first through the meeting of verse 10. A reader who has just come from Romans 3 hears the verse with a new ear. Paul says God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand, and did this so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25-26. The problem behind the psalm's forgiveness, in verse 2, is how a righteous God can lift away iniquity without ignoring it. The Old Testament people were forgiven on the basis of a mercy they could not see the price of. The cross shows the price. Love and faithfulness, mercy and truth, meet in one event, and neither has to give way to the other.

The second link is in the actual words. When John writes that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth, John 1:14, he chooses two nouns that are a natural translation of chesed and emet, the pair in verse 10 that had summarised the character of God since Sinai. He goes on, "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ," John 1:17. The meaning is that what the psalm imagined as two qualities meeting on a road has now become a Person walking among people. The verb in verse 9, "that His glory may dwell in our land," is the verb behind the tabernacle, and John's verb "made His dwelling" carries the same idea. The prayer that the glory of God would settle again in the land is answered when the Word tabernacles among us and we see His glory.

The third link is peace. The psalm promises that God will speak peace to His people, verse 8, and that righteousness and peace will kiss. Paul says Christ Himself is our peace, who has torn down the dividing wall of hostility and made peace through the cross, and that He came and preached peace to those far away and to those near, Ephesians 2:14-17. The phrase "far and near" is Isaiah's, from Isaiah 57:19. Luke's Gospel records the angels' word that on earth there is peace among those on whom God's favour rests, Luke 2:14, a phrase that takes up the word "favour" from verse 1. The risen Lord's first word to His disciples was peace, and He said that His peace is a gift the world cannot give, John 14:27. Acts 10:36 sums up the gospel as "the gospel of peace through Jesus Christ."

Fourth, the psalm points to Christ as the one who goes before and who follows. Righteousness precedes the LORD in verse 13 and prepares the path for His steps. The forerunner of the Gospels, John the Baptist, was sent to go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him, Luke 1:76, and Jesus then came as the one who is Himself the righteousness of God for those who believe, Romans 1:17. He is the meeting point for everything the psalm asks. The revival of verse 6, "that Your people may rejoice in You," is given when He raises sinners from death to life.

A note of care. The psalm has its own historical setting, and it should not be turned into a set of predictions. Its virtues are not personifications of Christ, and the kiss of verse 10 is not a code for a single event. The link is that the New Testament writers, when they explain what the cross achieved, reach for the vocabulary this psalm helped to shape. That is enough to hear the psalm as a witness. It is a prayer of a people who could not yet see the price of the mercy they were asking for, and who trusted it anyway.
study.god:
The psalm draws a portrait of God through the actions the people remember and the qualities they call on. The first quality is favour. Verse 1 begins with God showing favour to His land, and the word carries the sense of delight and acceptance. It suggests that God's first move toward His people is not suspicion but goodwill, and that the land itself is the object of His care. The rest of the psalm may plead for it to be renewed, but it never suggests that God's basic attitude has changed.

Second, God is a forgiver who does not ignore sin. The psalm uses three separate verbs in verses 2 and 3: He lifted, He covered, He withheld. The forgiveness is thorough, but it is also costly in the sense that sin has to be dealt with, not overlooked. The Sinai formula, Exodus 34:6-7, holds forgiveness and justice together in a single proclamation, and Psalm 85 depends on that. It also shows that God's anger is real. He has "burning anger" that He can turn from. This is not a deity who never becomes angry, but one whose anger is bounded by His mercy. Psalm 103:9 says He will not always accuse us, nor harbour His anger forever.

Third, God hears and speaks. The singer's decision to listen, verse 8, assumes a God who has a word to say and who says it to those who wait. The promised word is peace, shalom, a word of wholeness that touches every part of life. The God of this psalm is not silent, and He is not only a judge. He speaks to His people and to His saints, the practitioners of covenant love.

Fourth, God's attributes belong together. This is the great contribution of verse 10. Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss. One might have supposed that love wants to overlook what faithfulness must punish, or that righteousness demands what peace cannot afford. The psalm affirms that in God these are not competing but united, and it looks to the day when they are seen together. Psalm 89:14 confirms that they belong to the character of His rule: righteousness and justice are the foundation of His throne, and loving devotion and faithfulness go before Him. The God of the Bible is not an arbitrary mixture of severity and softness. He is one, and His qualities are consistent with one another.

Fifth, God is the giver of every good, verse 12. The land's increase is the LORD's gift. This affirms the doctrine of providence: the rain and the harvest are not natural accidents but expressions of His giving. Yet the giving is tied to the restored relationship. In the psalm, the land is fruitful because the God who forgives is now at home in it, so that His glory dwells there. This makes fertility a sign of presence.

Sixth, God is a God who requires, as well as gives. Those who fear Him, verse 9, are the ones for whom salvation is near, and those who are His people must not return to folly. Mercy does not cancel holiness. The moral shape of the psalm is that God takes back a people not to leave them as they were but to bring them into the peace of a righteous life.

For worship, the psalm gives believers a script for hard seasons: rehearse what God has done, ask plainly for more, wait for a word, and hold a picture of the finished work. It also teaches us to be careful about how we picture God. He is not a partial mercy or a partial justice, but full of both, and He does not sacrifice one for the other. That is why the cross is at once the greatest act of justice and the greatest act of love.

crossReferences.note: The plea 'Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved' is a refrain repeated in Psalm 80. It provides the prayer language behind Psalm 85:4. The face that shines is the opposite of the anger that burns, and both psalms ask God to turn from one to the other.

When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, the people were like dreamers, and then they asked for more restoration, like streams in the Negev. This is the closest sibling to Psalm 85. It shows the same two-step of thanks for a past turning and a plea for a further one, and it ends with the promise that those who sow in tears will reap in joy.

The LORD proclaims Himself compassionate and gracious, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Psalm 85 draws its vocabulary from this proclamation. It shows that verses 2, 3 and 10 are not new inventions but appeals to what God has said about Himself.

Moses quotes the Sinai description of God when he pleads for Israel's pardon after the rebellion at the border of the land. He asks God to forgive according to the greatness of His loving devotion, just as He has forgiven since Egypt. The psalmist prays in the same way, resting on God's past forgiveness as the ground for a new request.

Righteousness and justice are the foundation of God's throne, and loving devotion and faithfulness go before Him. This makes the same pairs as Psalm 85:10 and 85:13 characteristics of God's rule. The two psalms sit close together and read like two views of the same throne room.

The heavens are asked to drip down righteousness and the earth to open so that salvation may sprout and righteousness spring up with it. It is the same movement as Psalm 85:11, where righteousness looks down and faithfulness sprouts up. Isaiah ties it to the creating power of the LORD, who has made it.

The heavens have withheld their dew and the earth its crops, a picture of a land where blessing has not yet returned. This helps explain why Psalm 85:12 asks that the land yield its increase. The psalm's promise would have been especially precious to those who were farming in a season of drought.

As the second temple's foundation was laid, many shouted for joy and the older ones who remembered the first house wept, and the two sounds could not be told apart. The scene captures the mixture of thanks and ache in Psalm 85, where past restoration and present need sit side by side.

The Word became flesh, made His dwelling among us, and is full of grace and truth. The words for grace and truth fit chesed and emet in Psalm 85:10, and the verb for dwelling recalls the glory that dwells in the land, verse 9. John seems to be telling us that the psalm's hope has come to a person.

God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His righteousness, so that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. This is the New Testament's account of how the meeting of verse 10 is possible: righteousness and mercy are joined at the cross.

Christ is our peace, who has torn down the dividing wall and preached peace to those far and near. It picks up the promise that God will speak peace, Psalm 85:8, and shows that the peace He speaks is a person who reconciles Jew and Gentile to God in one body.

John the Baptist is to go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him. The line is close to the last verse of the psalm, where righteousness goes before Him to prepare the way for His steps. The Gospel supplies a forerunner in flesh and blood who does what the psalm's righteousness is said to do.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that runs through the whole Bible: how can a holy God live with a sinful people? The problem is stated in the opening chapters, where a man and a woman are sent from the garden and the way back is barred. It sharpens in Exodus, where God dwells among Israel in the tabernacle, and Israel promptly makes a golden calf. Moses then begs to see God's glory, and God passes before him and proclaims the name that Psalm 85 quotes, compassionate, gracious, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished, Exodus 34:6-7. From that point Israel's whole life depends on that name being true. The psalm is one of the places where it is tested in a later generation, when a returned people finds that forgiveness in the past does not remove the need for mercy in the present.

The psalm sets up the great question that the prophets sharpen. If God forgives and restores, and then His people fail again, what will make the restoration last? Isaiah answers that righteousness will rain down from the skies and salvation sprout from the earth, Isaiah 45:8. Ezekiel says that God will put His Spirit within them, Ezekiel 37:14. Jeremiah says that there will be a new covenant. The psalm belongs to this waiting. Its final verses do not describe a present reality; they hold a promise before the eyes of the people so that they can live toward it.

The promise is met in Christ. In Him the qualities of verse 10 are found together in a life, a death and a resurrection. He is the Word full of grace and truth, John 1:14. He makes peace by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:19-20. He is the righteousness that is revealed in the gospel, Romans 1:17, and He is the one who, through His forerunner, has been announced as the Lord who comes. In Him God's glory dwells among His people again, and in the church, the Spirit makes them a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:22.

The story reaches its end where the psalm looks. The apostle John hears the voice from the throne: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man," Revelation 21:3. The land that yields its increase becomes a new earth, and the peace that kisses righteousness becomes a world without war or curse. The prayer "Will You not revive us again" is answered by a people raised to a life that does not end. There the God who turned His anger away and turned His people back has finished the turning, and the path that righteousness opened has led all the way home.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist remember God doing for His people in verses 1-3?

options.text: He forgave their iniquity, covered their sin, and restrained His fury.
options.note: The opening verses recall a specific, past act of God's forgiveness and restraint of wrath.

options.text: He punished them without any relief.
options.note: The text describes forgiveness and restrained anger, not unrelieved punishment.

options.text: He restored Jacob from captivity.
options.note: This is true and part of what is remembered, verse 1, though the fuller emphasis in verses 2-3 is on forgiveness and restrained wrath.

options.text: He sent them into exile for the first time.
options.note: The psalm remembers restoration from captivity, not the beginning of exile.

quiz.q: What is the psalmist's central plea in verses 4-7?

options.text: That God would revive His people again and show them His loving devotion.
options.note: Verses 6-7 make the plea explicit: revive us again, show us Your loving devotion.

options.text: That God would give them more land.
options.note: The plea is for revival and renewed favor, not territorial expansion.

options.text: That God would punish their enemies immediately.
options.note: The psalm's focus is inward, pleading for the people's own revival, not judgment on enemies.

options.text: That God would put away His displeasure toward them.
options.note: This is a true part of the plea, verse 4, though the fuller request also includes revival, verse 6, and loving devotion, verse 7.

quiz.q: According to verse 8, what does the psalmist resolve to do?

options.text: Listen to what God the LORD will say, since He will speak peace to His people.
options.note: Verse 8 pictures the psalmist pausing to listen for God's word of peace.

options.text: Speak first and demand an answer from God.
options.note: The psalmist resolves to listen, not to demand.

options.text: Stop praying altogether.
options.note: The psalm continues in confident prayer, not silence.

options.text: Wait for God's salvation, since it is near to those who fear Him.
options.note: This truth appears in verse 9, closely related, though the specific resolve named in verse 8 is to listen for what God will say.

quiz.q: What beautiful picture appears in verse 10?

options.text: Loving devotion and faithfulness joining together; righteousness and peace kissing.
options.note: This is the psalm's climactic image of reconciled attributes meeting in blessing.

options.text: Two armies meeting in battle.
options.note: The image is one of reconciliation and embrace, not conflict.

options.text: The sun and moon standing still.
options.note: That image belongs elsewhere in Scripture, not this verse.

options.text: Faithfulness sprouting from the earth and righteousness looking down from heaven.
options.note: This closely related picture appears in verse 11, but verse 10 specifically pictures loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace meeting and kissing.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's vision of righteousness and peace meeting point to Christ?

options.text: It is fulfilled at the cross, where God's justice and mercy meet fully in Jesus.
options.note: Romans 3:25-26 shows God as both just and the justifier through Christ's atoning death.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The psalm's language is directly echoed in Paul's description of the cross.

options.text: It predicts the exact rebuilding date of the Jerusalem temple.
options.note: The psalm's vision is about reconciliation, not a construction timeline.

options.text: It anticipates a future, final peace for all creation.
options.note: This captures a true future dimension of the psalm's hope, but understates that its central fulfillment is already secured in Christ's finished work at the cross.

questions: The psalmist remembers God's past forgiveness before pleading for present revival. What past evidence of God's grace in your own life can fuel your prayers today?
Verse 6 asks, 'Will You not revive us again?' Where do you most need God to breathe fresh life into a tired or discouraged part of your faith?
The psalmist resolves to listen for what God will say rather than rushing ahead. What would it look like this week to wait and listen for God's word of peace instead of forcing your own solution?
Righteousness and peace kiss in verse 10, a picture fulfilled at the cross. How does knowing that God's justice and mercy have already met in Christ change how you come to Him with your own sin?
Righteousness goes before the LORD to prepare His way in verse 13. Where is God asking you to prepare the way for His work, in your own heart or in the lives of others?

translationNotes.note: Restored Jacob from captivity can also be rendered restored the fortunes of Jacob, a broader phrase that need not refer only to literal exile.
Kissed pictures loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace as personified figures embracing, a vivid image of full reconciliation.
Righteousness will go before Him pictures righteousness as a herald preparing the way for a king's arrival, language echoed in the ministry of John the Baptist.
